title: Entropy
question: Why does time run only one way?
objectives: Explain entropy as a count of the arrangements that match what you see
State the second law and say why local order does not break it
Explain why some processes never run backwards

key_terms.definition: A measure of how many hidden arrangements of particles produce the same outward state. More arrangements means higher entropy.
The entropy of the universe never decreases in any process.
A change that raises total entropy and so does not undo itself, such as a gas spreading out or heat flowing from hot to cold.

guess.prompt: A hundred gas molecules bounce around a box. What are the odds that, at one given moment, all 100 are in the left half?

options.text: Far less than 1 in a billion billion billion

guess.reveal: Far less. Each molecule has two choices, so there are 2 multiplied by itself 100 times arrangements, a 1 followed by 30 zeros, and only one of them has every molecule on the left.

hook: A cup of coffee cools down and never heats itself back up. An egg breaks and never unbreaks. No law of motion forbids the reverse. So why does it never happen?

explanation.body_md:
Everything you can see is made of a vast number of particles, and the same outward state can be produced by many different hidden arrangements of them.

**Entropy** is a measure of how many. A state that can be made in more ways has higher entropy.

Take four molecules in a box and ask how many are in the left half.

| In the left half | Arrangements |
| --- | --- |
| 4 | 1 |
| 3 | 4 |
| 2 | 6 |
| 1 | 4 |
| 0 | 1 |

An even split is the most likely result, simply because it can happen in the most ways. With the huge numbers of molecules in real things, spread-out arrangements outnumber bunched-up ones so heavily that bunching is never seen.

That is why gas fills a room, and why heat flows from hot to cold: both changes move to states with more arrangements.

The **second law of thermodynamics** sums it up. The entropy of the universe never decreases. Changes that raise it do not undo themselves, and that one-way rule is what separates the past from the future.
explanation.analogy: A new deck of cards is in one special order. Shuffle it and it ends up disordered. Shuffling does not aim at disorder. There is one sorted order and an astronomical number of unsorted ones, so almost anything you do lands on an unsorted one.
takeaways: Entropy counts the arrangements that match what you see.
Systems drift to high entropy because those states can happen in vastly more ways.
Total entropy never falls, which is why some changes never run backwards.

visual.alt: Bar chart for four molecules: one arrangement has all four on the left, four have three, six have two, four have one and one has none
visual.caption: An even split can happen in the most ways.

worked_example.body_md:
Drop 50 grams of ice at 0 degrees Celsius into a room at 20 degrees and wait.

1. The ice melts and warms. Its molecules go from fixed sites to moving freely, so its entropy rises, by about 76.3 joules per kelvin.
2. The heat came from the room. Losing heat lowers the room's entropy, by about 71.7.
3. Add them. The total rises by about 4.6.

So entropy went down in one place and the second law was still obeyed, because the law is about the total. The total rose, and that is also why the reverse never happens: warm water in a warm room does not turn itself back into ice.

misconception.claim: Living things and freezers break the second law, because they create order.
misconception.correction_md:
The second law is about the total entropy of everything involved, not about one object. A freezer orders the water inside it and pushes more than enough heat out of its back to make up for it. A plant builds ordered tissue while increasing entropy in its surroundings by more. Entropy can fall in one place whenever it rises by more somewhere else.

A related slip is to treat entropy as plain messiness. Disorder is a useful first picture, but what is actually being measured is a count of arrangements.

recall_items.prompt: In one sentence, what does entropy measure?
recall_items.answer: How many hidden arrangements of particles produce the same outward state.

recall_items.prompt: The second law says that the entropy of the ___ never decreases.
Why does a gas spread to fill its container?

options.text: Nature prefers things to be untidy
Far more arrangements are spread out than bunched up

recall_items.explanation: Nothing pushes the gas outward. Spread-out arrangements simply outnumber the rest.

recall_items.prompt: For 4 molecules in a box, how many of the 16 arrangements have exactly 2 in each half?
Your freezer turns water into ice, which is more ordered. Why is that not a violation of the second law?
recall_items.answer: The law is about total entropy. The freezer releases heat into the kitchen, raising entropy there by more than it falls in the ice.

recall_items.prompt: True or false: the entropy of an object can never decrease.
recall_items.explanation: Only the total cannot decrease. The room that melts the ice loses entropy.

recall_items.prompt: Why does a broken egg never reassemble, even though no law of motion forbids it?
recall_items.answer: There are overwhelmingly more broken arrangements than whole ones, so a move back to a whole egg is possible in principle and never seen in practice.

recall_items.prompt: Which has higher entropy, 1 kg of ice at 0 degrees or 1 kg of water at 0 degrees? Why?
recall_items.answer: The water. Its molecules move about freely, so far more arrangements are possible than in the fixed sites of ice.

rubric.point: Entropy counts the arrangements of particles that match the outward state.
States with more arrangements are overwhelmingly more likely, so systems move toward them.
The second law: total entropy never decreases.
The reverse is not forbidden by the laws of motion, only so unlikely that it is never seen.

false_claims: Says the entropy of any single object can never fall
Says particles are pushed toward disorder by a force

challenge.prompt: A deck of 52 cards can be put in about 8 followed by 67 zeros different orders. Suppose you shuffled once a second for a billion years, which is about 3 followed by 16 zeros seconds. Roughly what fraction of all the orders would you have seen?
model_answer: Divide the number of shuffles by the number of orders: 3 × 10^16 divided by 8 × 10^67.
That is about 4 × 10^-52, which is a decimal point followed by 51 zeros and then a 4.
So you would have seen practically none of them, and the chance of landing on the sorted order is as good as zero.
challenge.follow_up: A cup of coffee contains far more molecules than a deck has cards. What does that tell you about the odds of it reheating itself?

connections.body_md: When Claude Shannon measured information in the 1940s, his formula had the same mathematical form as the one for entropy, and he used the same name. Both count possibilities: how many arrangements a system could be in, or how many messages could have been sent.

An engine turns heat into motion by letting heat flow from hot to cold. The second law sets a ceiling on how much of that heat can become work. An engine that turned all of it into work would lower total entropy, which cannot happen.

deep_dive.body_md:
**Two ways to meet entropy**

Entropy was first defined through heat. When a quantity of heat flows into something at a steady temperature, its entropy rises by that heat divided by the temperature. That definition lets engineers calculate, but it does not tell you what entropy is.

The second way is to count. Any object you can see is made of an enormous number of particles, and the same outward appearance can be produced by many different hidden arrangements of them. Entropy tracks how many. A state that can be made in more ways has higher entropy. This is the view this lesson uses, because once you can count you can see why the second law holds.

**Counting with four molecules**

Put four molecules in a box and ask only how many are in the left half. Each molecule is either left or right, so there are 16 possible arrangements. One of them has all four on the left. Four have three on the left. Six have two on each side. An even split is the most likely result for no deeper reason than that it can happen in the most ways.

Now scale up. With 100 molecules there are about 1.3 million million million million million arrangements, a 1 followed by 30 zeros, and exactly one has every molecule on the left. A real box of air holds vastly more than 100 molecules. The bunched-up arrangements are not forbidden. They are so heavily outnumbered that you will never see one.

The physicist Ludwig Boltzmann (1844 to 1906) turned this counting into a formula. The entropy of a state is a constant multiplied by the logarithm of the number of arrangements that produce it, written S = k ln W. More ways, more entropy.

**Why gas spreads and heat flows**

Remove a divider and a gas fills the whole box. It occupies a larger volume, a larger volume allows more arrangements, and so its entropy has gone up. The process is irreversible: the gas will not gather itself back.

Heat flowing from hot to cold is the same story. The combined system has more arrangements available when the energy is shared out than when it is concentrated, so sharing is what you observe. Melting shows it too. In a solid the molecules sit at fixed sites. In a liquid they move about more freely, so the liquid has the higher entropy.

**The second law, and what it allows**

The second law of thermodynamics says that the entropy of the universe never decreases in any process. Irreversible processes increase it.

The law is about the total, and that is where people go wrong. A freezer makes ice, which is more ordered than water. A growing plant builds ordered tissue. Neither breaks the law, because each one increases entropy somewhere else by more than it reduces it locally.

A worked case makes this concrete. Put 50 grams of ice at 0 degrees Celsius in a room at 20 degrees and let it melt and warm up. The ice gains about 76.3 joules per kelvin of entropy. The room, which supplied the heat, loses about 71.7. The total goes up by about 4.6. One part lost entropy, and the whole still gained.

**Absolute zero**

As something is cooled toward absolute zero its entropy falls toward a minimum and it approaches perfect order. The third law of thermodynamics says absolute zero can never actually be reached in a finite number of steps. Experiments have come within about one ten-billionth of a degree.

**Time's arrow**

The laws that govern single collisions between molecules work the same forwards and backwards. Entropy is where a direction enters. Because there are overwhelmingly more high-entropy arrangements than low-entropy ones, systems move from the rare kind to the common kind and do not come back. Physicists call this the arrow of time. A film of an egg breaking looks wrong in reverse because the reverse runs from many arrangements to few.

**A word about the word disorder**

Textbooks often say entropy measures disorder, and you can use that as a first handle: a shuffled deck is more disordered than a new one. But messy is a judgement people make. Number of arrangements is something you can count. When the two disagree, trust the count.
